_comment: How Chinese's phrases hold together, for lib/chunker.py. Simplified characters, which is what zh teaches; nothing here would change for a traditional source, because every rule below is about punctuation and particles and the two scripts share both.
_closes:
CHINESE IS CUT AT ITS OWN PUNCTUATION, AND ALMOST NOWHERE ELSE. Japanese is read in bunsetsu and its particles say where one ends, so lib/lang/ja.chunk.json can list は が を に and be right; Chinese has no case particles at all, and the only marks it writes that reliably end a sense group are the ones it prints. That is less of a loss than it sounds: a Chinese sentence is punctuated at every clause -- the comma splice that a European editor would strike out is the ordinary way to build a Chinese sentence -- so the marks fall about where the breath does. Measured on 从前，在一个小村子里，住着一个老人和他的孙子。 the cut is 从前， | 在一个小村子里， | 住着一个老人和他的孙子。 and on 他一边喝着茶，一边看着报纸；外面下着雨。 it is 他一边喝着茶， | 一边看着报纸； | 外面下着雨。 -- three sense groups each, none of them cut through anything.
The mark stays with the chunk BEFORE it, because the cut is made after the match; the closing brackets 」』）》】 are in the list for the same reason the full stop is, and they are what makes 「你好。」他说。 come out as 「你好。」 | 他说。 rather than whole (the full stop inside the quotation closes nothing, since a bracket is not a content character).
吗 呢 吧 ARE HERE FOR THE CAPTIONS. They end a sentence, and after a sentence-final particle a Chinese source almost always prints a mark, which closes the chunk before they are ever reached -- so in a book they earn nothing. In an ASR caption, which is punctuated by nobody, they are the only thing left: 你去过北京吗我没去过 cuts as 你去过北京吗 | 我没去过, and without them it is one chunk of ten characters. The price is a word that begins with one of them, 吗啡 and 呢子 being the whole of the list worth naming; 他吸了吗啡 comes out 他吸了吗 | 啡, which is a wrong boundary in a word this series will not meet twice.
_not_the_aspect_particles:
了 着 过 WERE TRIED AND ARE DELIBERATELY NOT HERE, and this is the entry to read before adding them back. They look like the Japanese particles and are not: they close the verb, not the phrase, and the thing that follows them is the verb's own object. Measured with them in the list: 门开着，外面下着雨。 cuts as 门开着， | 外面下着 | 雨。 and 我昨天去了北京，看了一个朋友。 as 我昨天去了 | 北京， | 看了 | 一个朋友。 -- a verb parted from its object every time, and a Chinese object is very often the one character that is left standing alone. Punctuation alone gives 外面下着雨。 whole, which is what a reader should meet.
They also break WORDS, because Chinese offers no signal that a character starts a new one: 我了解他的想法。 cut after 了 gives 我了 | 解他的想法。, and 着急 过去 过程 为了 除了 fail the same way. That much can be bought off -- longest match wins, so listing 了解 着急 过去 过程 as closers of their own turns each trap into a cut after the whole word, and it was measured doing exactly that -- but it fixes the smaller half of the fault and leaves the verb and its object parted, so nothing was kept.
的 IS NOT HERE either, for the reason ja.chunk.json gives for の: it binds a modifier to its head (我的书, 红色的花), and this toolbox never splits those. 和 或 但是 are not here because they OPEN the clause they introduce, and `closes` is the only lever this format has -- a list of things to cut AFTER cannot say `cut before`. Both are left to the model, which reads the sentence; the offline cut is offered as a choice and never imposed.
_opens_content: A mark only ENDS a phrase when something that can begin one comes after it: a Han character, a Latin word, a number, or an opening bracket. What this keeps out is the case Chinese has and Japanese does not -- a second mark (。」), or a particle that leans backwards. 的 了 着 过 吗 呢 吧 are excluded by name: a chunk that began with any of them would open on a word's second half or on a particle glossing into nothing.
_max_chars: DISABLED ON PURPOSE, and the key is kept only so that the next reader knows it was weighed. In Japanese this is the escape hatch for a run of hiragana with no content word in it: past this many characters a particle may close a phrase even though what follows is not a content character. In Chinese `not a content character' means punctuation or a particle, and there is no sentence long enough to make cutting before a comma right -- the mark would open the next chunk instead of closing this one. A long chunk is the better failure, so this is set past any sentence the toolbox will see.
_grow_to: How many characters (the punctuation not counted) two neighbouring pieces may come to and still be joined into one chunk, where pkuseg's part-of-speech model cuts the sentence into words (below). Six and not Japanese's eight: a Chinese character carries about what a Japanese word does, and the hand-made chunks of this toolbox's Chinese fixtures run from two characters to six (老人去河边, 我想要一杯茶).
_tags: WITH PKUSEG'S PART-OF-SPEECH MODEL INSTALLED (lib/words.py tagger_available; ./install.sh fetches it) a Chinese sentence is not cut at its punctuation alone. It is cut between the words the word strip shows, by the tag pkuseg gives each (lib/chunker.py _zh_seams): a coverb binds its object and 的 its head, a measure word its number and its noun, an adverb the verb after it; a verb takes its object; and where a verb or a coverb has already come in the clause, the noun before the next verb closes a phrase. The pieces then grow while two neighbours fit in grow_to characters. That is what cuts a clause nobody punctuated -- the auto-captions' whole case -- which the list above leaves in one piece. Without the model, the list above is the whole of the cut.
_the_last_five: These five belong to the DICTIONARY path in lib/chunker.py, which a `closes` list turns off: an unspaced language with one is cut from its characters and never asks the word list, so none of them runs while the list above exists. They are written down all the same, because they are what the language is and what the fallback would use if the list were ever emptied. np_head `final': the modifier comes first (红花, 我的书, 这本书), so it attaches forward to the noun it modifies. adposition `before': Chinese governs with coverbs, which are verbs standing where a preposition stands and precede their object (在家, 跟他, 从北京, 把书) -- the exception is the localizer, which follows (桌子上, 屋子里), and 在桌子上 has one of each, which is more than the two-valued key can say. bind_forward `的$': the particle that makes everything before it into a modifier of what comes after, exactly Persian's ezafe in another script. min 2 / max 5 are words and not characters, and a Chinese word averages a character and a half, so they come to the same 2-8 characters the annotator is asked for in docs/lang/zh.md.
